theme: Who may dwell on your holy hill?
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 15. It is short, with only five verses, and it asks a question that the tabernacle readings have raised again and again. Read it as a response to the instructions for the tent: who is fit to enter?
settingTheScene: Psalm 15 is attributed to David. It begins with a question that fits the setting of worship at the sanctuary: “O LORD, who shall sojourn in your tent? Who shall dwell on your holy hill?” The “tent” and “holy hill” are the tabernacle and Jerusalem. After a week spent in the instructions for the tabernacle, this psalm answers from the point of view of a worshiper. It may have been used as an entrance liturgy, a set of questions asked at the gate by the priests.
observation: The question: “O LORD, who shall sojourn in your tent? Who shall dwell on your holy hill?” (v. 1).
The answer begins: “He who walks blamelessly and does what is right and speaks truth in his heart” (v. 2).
The person “does not slander with his tongue and does no evil to his neighbor, nor takes up a reproach against his friend” (v. 3).
He despises “a vile person” and honors “those who fear the LORD” (v. 4).
He “swears to his own hurt and does not change” (v. 4).
He does not put out his money at interest or take a bribe against the innocent (v. 5).
The psalm ends with a promise: “He who does these things shall never be moved” (v. 5).
interpretation:
The psalm asks the question every worshiper of the tabernacle had to ask: who is allowed in? The answer is not about ritual. It is about character, and most of it is about how a person treats other people. Truthfulness, honesty in speech, faithfulness to promises, and fairness in money are the marks of someone who belongs in God’s presence. The list is surprisingly practical. It is a picture of integrity in daily life.

Notice that the list begins and ends with a general statement: someone who “walks blamelessly” will “never be moved.” The portrait is of a person whose inner life and outer life match. “Speaks truth in his heart” means that his words are the same as his thoughts. He does not say one thing and mean another.

It is wise to read this psalm with the laws of Leviticus in view. The sacrifices did not replace the call to live rightly. God never wanted offerings from people who ignored their neighbors. The prophets will say the same thing later. A sacrifice offered by someone who lies, slanders, and cheats is an insult.

But we must be honest. If we read this psalm as a checklist, we all fail. None of us walks blamelessly. Taken seriously, the psalm brings us to the same place as the tabernacle: we need someone to qualify us. The question is still open, and the next psalm will make it sharper.
connection: Jesus is the only one who truly walked blamelessly, and who spoke truth in his heart. He is the one who can dwell on God’s holy hill, and he brings his people with him. Isaiah 33:14-16 asks a similar question and gives a similar answer. Paul says that we have been made “holy and blameless before him” in Christ (Ephesians 1:4). Hebrews 12:22 says that we have come to “Mount Zion and to the city of the living God.”
application:
Read the list in verses 2 to 5 slowly. Pick one item where you feel convicted, and confess it.

Ask whether your speech is honest. Is there something you have said recently that was not quite true?

Thank God that in Christ you are welcome in his tent, not because you pass the list, but because Jesus did.
prayerPrompts: Ask yourself honestly who may dwell on God’s holy hill, and tell him what you find.
Thank Jesus for walking blamelessly and bringing you in.
Ask him to make you truthful, faithful, and fair.
